mcqs.question: What interface must a class implement to create a thread using the Runnable approach?

options.B: Runnable
options.D: Callable

mcqs.explanation: The Runnable interface has one method: public void run(). Implementing it: class MyTask implements Runnable { public void run() { ... } }. Then: Thread t = new Thread(new MyTask()); t.start();

mcqs.question: Which Thread class method makes a thread sleep for 500 milliseconds?

options.B: Thread.delay(500)
options.D: Thread.pause(500)

mcqs.explanation: Thread.sleep(500) suspends the current thread for 500ms. It's a static method called as Thread.sleep(ms). It throws InterruptedException which must be handled or declared.

mcqs.question: What is the minimum thread priority value in Java?
mcqs.explanation: Thread priorities range from MIN_PRIORITY (1) to MAX_PRIORITY (10), with NORM_PRIORITY (5) as the default. These are static constants in the Thread class.

mcqs.question: What is the normal (default) thread priority?
mcqs.explanation: Thread.NORM_PRIORITY = 5 is the default priority for all threads. It falls in the middle of the MIN_PRIORITY(1) to MAX_PRIORITY(10) range.

mcqs.question: What is the maximum thread priority value in Java?
mcqs.explanation: Thread.MAX_PRIORITY = 10 is the highest thread priority. Set with t.setPriority(Thread.MAX_PRIORITY). Higher priority hints to the scheduler to prefer this thread, though actual behavior is OS-dependent.

mcqs.question: Which method checks if a thread is still alive (running or waiting)?

options.B: isActive()
options.D: hasStarted()

mcqs.explanation: t.isAlive() returns true if the thread has been started and has not yet terminated. It returns false before start() is called or after run() completes.

mcqs.question: What exception does Thread.sleep() throw?

options.B: SleepException
options.D: TimeoutException

mcqs.explanation: Thread.sleep() throws InterruptedException if the sleeping thread is interrupted by another thread calling thread.interrupt(). The caller must handle or declare this checked exception.

mcqs.question: What does thread.getName() return?

options.A: The thread's priority as a string
options.B: The name of the thread (e.g., 'Thread-0', or the name set by setName())
options.C: The class name of the runnable
options.D: The thread's ID number

mcqs.explanation: getName() returns the thread's name. Default names are Thread-0, Thread-1, etc. You can set a custom name: t.setName('WorkerThread') and retrieve it with t.getName().

mcqs.question: In the Runnable approach, what is passed to the Thread constructor?

options.A: The class name as a String
options.B: A Runnable object (the task to execute)
options.D: The thread priority

mcqs.explanation: Thread constructor accepts a Runnable: Thread t = new Thread(new MyTask()); or Thread t = new Thread(() -> { ... }); (lambda). The Thread executes the Runnable's run() method in the new thread when start() is called.

mcqs.question: What is synchronization in multithreading?

options.A: Making all threads run at the same speed
options.B: Coordinating access to shared resources so only one thread accesses them at a time
options.C: Synchronizing the system clock across threads
options.D: Starting all threads simultaneously

mcqs.explanation: Synchronization controls concurrent access to shared resources. By using synchronized methods or blocks, only one thread can access the critical section at a time, preventing race conditions and data corruption.

mcqs.question: What is the difference between a synchronized method and a synchronized block?

options.A: No difference — both lock the same thing
options.B: synchronized method locks the entire object (this); synchronized block can specify a different lock object, allowing finer-grained locking
options.C: synchronized block is not supported in Java
options.D: synchronized method is faster always

mcqs.explanation: synchronized void method() { } locks 'this' for the entire method. synchronized(lockObject) { ... } allows specifying exactly what to lock and for how long. Finer-grained locking reduces contention: two synchronized blocks on different lock objects can execute concurrently.

mcqs.question: What does wait() do in Java multithreading?

options.A: Makes the thread wait for sleep() to finish
options.B: Releases the object's lock and suspends the thread until notify() or notifyAll() wakes it
options.C: Blocks all other threads from starting
options.D: Waits for the thread to finish (like join)

mcqs.explanation: wait() must be called from a synchronized block. It releases the monitor lock on the object and puts the thread in a waiting state. It wakes when another thread calls notify() or notifyAll() on the same object, or when interrupted.

mcqs.question: What does notify() do in Java multithreading?

options.B: Wakes up ONE waiting thread that is waiting on the same object's monitor
options.D: Sends a message to a thread

mcqs.explanation: notify() wakes up exactly one thread waiting on the object's monitor (chosen arbitrarily by JVM). notifyAll() wakes ALL waiting threads. Both must be called from a synchronized block. The awakened thread must re-acquire the lock before continuing.

mcqs.question: What is the purpose of using 'implements Runnable' over 'extends Thread'?

options.A: Runnable allows you to set thread priority
options.B: Since Java has single inheritance, Runnable allows your class to still extend another class
options.D: Runnable provides more methods than Thread

mcqs.explanation: Java only allows extending one class. If you extend Thread, you can't extend any other class. Implementing Runnable separates 'what to execute' from 'how to execute it', following good OOP design and allowing your task class to inherit from another domain class.

mcqs.question: How does thread.setPriority(Thread.MAX_PRIORITY) affect thread execution?

options.A: Guarantees this thread always runs first
options.B: Gives a hint to the scheduler to prefer this thread — not a guarantee, depends on OS scheduler
options.C: Allocates more memory to this thread
options.D: Makes the thread run on a dedicated CPU core

mcqs.explanation: Priority is a scheduling hint, not a guarantee. Most OS schedulers consider priority, but a low-priority thread can still run if high-priority threads are waiting for I/O. Never rely on thread priorities for correctness — use synchronization mechanisms instead.

mcqs.question: What is a thread pool and why is it beneficial?

options.B: A managed set of reusable worker threads that process tasks from a queue, avoiding expensive thread creation/destruction for each task
options.C: A pool of memory allocated to threads
options.D: Multiple threads sharing a single run() method

mcqs.explanation: Creating/destroying threads for each task is expensive. Thread pools maintain a set of worker threads. Tasks are submitted to a queue; idle workers pick them up. Java provides Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) and other pool types. Pools improve performance and provide resource control.

mcqs.question: What does Thread.interrupt() do to a sleeping thread?

options.B: Causes the sleeping thread's Thread.sleep() to throw InterruptedException
options.D: Changes the thread's priority to minimum

mcqs.explanation: interrupt() sets the thread's interrupt flag. If the thread is sleeping (sleep()), waiting (wait()), or joining (join()), those methods throw InterruptedException. The thread can then handle the interruption gracefully — typically by stopping its work and exiting run().

mcqs.question: What does Thread.yield() do?

options.B: Hints to the scheduler that the current thread is willing to pause to let other threads of equal priority run
options.D: Increases thread priority temporarily

mcqs.explanation: Thread.yield() is a hint to the scheduler: 'I'm willing to give up CPU time'. It may allow other same-priority threads to run. It's not guaranteed to do anything — the scheduler can ignore it. Rarely used in practice.

mcqs.question: In what situation would you use notifyAll() instead of notify()?

options.A: When you want to wake only one thread
options.B: When multiple threads may be waiting for different conditions on the same object — notifyAll() ensures the right one eventually runs
options.C: notifyAll() is always preferred over notify()
options.D: When notify() doesn't work

mcqs.explanation: notify() wakes one waiting thread (arbitrary choice). If threads wait for different conditions, notifying just one might wake the wrong thread (it checks its condition, finds it false, waits again). notifyAll() wakes all — each checks its condition and the correct one proceeds. Safer but less efficient.

mcqs.question: What happens if you call start() on a Thread that has already been started?

options.A: A new thread is created and the old one stops
options.B: IllegalThreadStateException is thrown
options.C: The run() method is called again from the beginning
options.D: The thread restarts from its current position

mcqs.explanation: A Thread can only be started once. Calling start() on an already-started Thread (regardless of whether it's running or finished) throws IllegalThreadStateException. To run the same task again, create a new Thread object.

mcqs.question: What is the 'happens-before' guarantee provided by entering and exiting a synchronized block?

options.A: Code in synchronized blocks runs faster
options.B: All writes by Thread A before releasing a monitor are guaranteed to be visible to Thread B after it acquires the same monitor
options.D: All threads share the same cache when synchronized

mcqs.explanation: Java Memory Model: releasing a monitor (exiting synchronized) happens-before acquiring the same monitor. Thread A's writes before unlock are guaranteed visible to Thread B after lock. Without this guarantee, Thread B might see stale cached values. synchronized provides both mutual exclusion AND memory visibility.

mcqs.question: Why is the 'double-checked locking' pattern with non-volatile fields broken in Java?

options.B: Without volatile, the JVM/CPU may reorder instructions so another thread sees a partially-constructed object through the non-null reference before its fields are initialized
options.C: It requires synchronized at both check points
options.D: It only works with primitive types

mcqs.explanation: if(instance == null) { synchronized(this) { if(instance == null) { instance = new Singleton(); } } } — without volatile on 'instance', the JVM may publish the reference before the object is fully constructed (instruction reordering). Another thread sees non-null but gets a partially initialized object. The fix: declare instance as volatile.

mcqs.question: What is 'livelock' and how does it differ from deadlock?

options.B: In deadlock, threads are blocked waiting; in livelock, threads are actively changing state in response to each other but making no progress — like two people in a corridor each stepping aside the same way
options.D: Livelock involves only one thread; deadlock involves multiple

mcqs.explanation: Deadlock: threads blocked indefinitely (no state change). Livelock: threads keep changing state (active) but no progress — they respond to each other repeatedly in a way that prevents completion. Example: two threads each release a lock when they detect the other wants it, then both immediately re-acquire, causing infinite back-and-forth.

mcqs.question: What is 'false sharing' in multithreaded Java programs on multi-core processors?

options.B: When two threads access different variables that happen to be on the same CPU cache line, causing frequent cache invalidations and degrading performance
options.C: Sharing objects that shouldn't be shared
options.D: Thread synchronization overhead

mcqs.explanation: CPU caches operate in cache lines (~64 bytes). If Thread 1 writes variable A and Thread 2 writes variable B, and A and B are in the same cache line, each write invalidates the other CPU's cache line — even though they're modifying different variables. Fix: pad variables to separate cache lines. @Contended annotation addresses this in Java.

mcqs.question: What advantage does ReentrantLock (java.util.concurrent) have over synchronized blocks?

options.B: ReentrantLock supports tryLock() (non-blocking attempt), lockInterruptibly() (interruptible waiting), fair mode (FIFO ordering), and multiple condition variables — more flexible than synchronized
options.D: ReentrantLock doesn't require unlock()

mcqs.explanation: synchronized is simple but limited. ReentrantLock adds: tryLock() — attempt to acquire without blocking (try different approach if failed); lockInterruptibly() — wait for lock but allow interruption; new ReentrantLock(true) — fair mode ensures FIFO ordering; lock.newCondition() — multiple condition queues on one lock. Must always unlock in finally block.

mcqs.question: What is 'thread-confinement' as a thread safety strategy?

options.A: Restricting threads to specific CPU cores
options.B: Ensuring a piece of data is only ever accessed by one thread — no sharing means no synchronization needed
options.C: Confining threads to a specific JVM memory region
options.D: Using ThreadGroup to restrict thread access

mcqs.explanation: Thread-confinement: data 'owned' by one thread is never shared. No sharing → no need for synchronization → no race conditions. Patterns: stack-confined (local variables accessed only in their method's stack frame), ThreadLocal (per-thread copy), message-passing architectures (Akka actors). The simplest thread safety strategy.

mcqs.question: In the Executor framework, what is the difference between execute() and submit()?

options.B: execute() runs a Runnable with no return value; submit() accepts Runnable or Callable and returns a Future for retrieving results or handling exceptions
options.D: execute() uses multiple threads; submit() uses one

mcqs.explanation: executor.execute(runnable) — fire-and-forget, no way to check result or exception. executor.submit(callable) returns Future<T> — call future.get() to wait for result and receive checked exceptions. submit() with Runnable returns Future<Void>. submit() is preferred when you need results or exception tracking.

mcqs.question: What does ConcurrentHashMap offer over Collections.synchronizedMap(HashMap) for thread safety?

options.B: ConcurrentHashMap allows concurrent reads and fine-grained segment locking (not locking entire map for writes) — much higher throughput under concurrent access
options.D: ConcurrentHashMap only allows one write at a time

mcqs.explanation: synchronizedMap wraps every operation in synchronized — only one thread can do ANYTHING at a time. ConcurrentHashMap (Java 8+) uses CAS and segment/bucket-level locking: multiple writers can work on different buckets simultaneously; reads are lock-free. Under high concurrency, ConcurrentHashMap has dramatically higher throughput.

mcqs.question: What is the 'atomic' guarantee, and why is AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() truly atomic while counter++ is not?

options.A: Both are atomic — Java guarantees all operations are atomic
options.B: counter++ is read-modify-write (3 non-atomic steps); incrementAndGet() uses a single CAS CPU instruction that either succeeds atomically or retries — the JVM never sees a partial update
options.D: counter++ is atomic for int but not long

mcqs.explanation: counter++ compiles to: GETFIELD, IADD, PUTFIELD — three bytecode instructions. A thread switch between any two allows another thread to see an inconsistent state. incrementAndGet() uses compareAndSet in a loop: read current value, add 1, write IF value still equals what was read (CAS). Hardware executes CAS atomically in one instruction — truly indivisible.

mcqs.question: How do virtual threads (Project Loom, Java 19+) fundamentally change Java's multithreading model?

options.A: Virtual threads are identical to platform threads
options.B: Virtual threads are lightweight JVM-managed threads (millions possible) that are multiplexed onto fewer OS threads; they block without blocking the underlying OS thread, enabling massive concurrency without thread pools
options.C: Virtual threads eliminate the need for synchronization
options.D: Virtual threads only work on multi-core machines

mcqs.explanation: Traditional Java threads (platform threads) = one-to-one OS threads (~1MB stack). Virtual threads (JDK 21): JVM manages scheduling; when a virtual thread blocks (I/O, sleep), the OS thread is released to run other virtual threads. You can create millions of virtual threads. This eliminates the need for reactive programming patterns for I/O-bound workloads.
